操作時先以蒸汽鍋爐或壓縮空氣供氣，再以鍵盤、紙卷或數位音樂介面控制閥門，使氣流進: Playing starts with steam from a boiler or with compressed air; a keyboard, a paper roll or a digital music interface then works the valves, so that the air passes into the whistles and sounds. For a beginner the work is pitch, rhythm and duration, because timbre and volume cannot be changed; with the steam type the pitch depends on temperature and the instrument has to be retuned again and again. The player works a keyboard, and the instrument usually sits on a boat, a circus wagon or a trailer.

汽笛琴主要用於美國河船與馬戲團場合，以蒸汽或壓縮空氣驅動哨音，可由鍵盤或音樂卷筒: The calliope is used mainly on American riverboats and in circus settings, driven by steam or compressed air, played from a keyboard or a music roll, and on some instruments from a digital music interface. In recordings and on screen, Henry Mancini's song uses the calliope to suggest a circus atmosphere; the Beatles used a calliope recording to set a circus scene; and the first season of Mission: Impossible also used calliope music from a travelling circus as background.
汽笛琴以蒸汽或壓縮空氣吹動大型汽笛發聲，音量極大，部分小型者亦可在數里外聽見。演: The calliope sounds by blowing steam or compressed air through large whistles, and it is extremely loud: some small instruments can be heard several miles away. The player cannot change the timbre or the volume; the improved Denny type is the exception, controlling steam pressure to vary the volume. Musical expression is limited to pitch, rhythm and duration. Its whistles are tuned chromatically and there may be twenty-five to sixty-seven of them, thirty-two on a traditional steam instrument; the pitch depends on the steam temperature, and the upper register often goes out of tune, which became a hallmark. Unlike a mechanical organ, it sounds with whistles.
汽笛琴由麻薩諸塞州伍斯特的 Joshua C. Stoddard 於 1855: The calliope was patented in 1855 by Joshua C. Stoddard of Worcester, Massachusetts, and the idea can be traced back to the 1832 steam trumpet. It began as a signal device for railways and ships and then moved onto paddle steamers. In 1859 Arthur S. Denny showed an improved model at the Crystal Palace in London, but it did not catch on. From the 1900s it was played automatically from paper rolls, and compressed air gradually replaced steam. Thomas J. Nichol of Cincinnati built many surviving instruments between 1890 and 1932; from 1985 David Morecraft revived steam construction. After the middle of the twentieth century, as steam power declined, most of the instruments disappeared.
汽笛琴的發聲體為大型哨子，最初使用火車哨子。蒸汽型常見黃銅鍵盤，以耐熱、耐濕並呈: The calliope sounds with large whistles, originally train whistles. Steam instruments usually have a brass keyboard, chosen for its resistance to heat and damp and its highly polished sheen. The whistle resonators include rolled copper sheet, and cast bronze or brass is also found. Some self-mounted instruments sit on a carved, painted and gilded wagon. The source does not say what the case, the boiler and the other parts are made of.
汽笛琴（Calliope）是美國氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號: The calliope is an American aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.222.11, sounded by blowing steam or compressed air through large whistles; it is usually very loud, cannot change timbre or volume, and can control only pitch, rhythm and duration. It can be played from a keyboard by a performer, or automatically from a mechanical roll. In the steam age it was used mostly on riverboats and in circuses, and in circus parades it usually came last.
